name: Emeka Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This interview is confidential. What does an ordinary day at the contact centre look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43, have a two-year college diploma, and lead the delivery complaints queue at the contact centre. I am good at finding the one scan that explains why a parcel went to the wrong door. I earn the usual wage for this job and train agents on the awkward calls. I do not use AI tools; I open the delivery record myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is on your mind after you leave work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife, Rina, and I have two children in school and a mortgage. She helps in a school kitchen, and we have roughly five months of expenses saved. There are some other contact centres close enough to try, though I would have to learn their rotas. I still remember a customer who lost a birthday parcel because we trusted the wrong door photograph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau sounds like the small sorter the office keeps offering us. I would rather check a door photograph against the street number before closing a claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my work remains and our five-month reserve covers a normal surprise. Rina’s school kitchen hours are regular in term time, but I still count on my wage for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading delivery complaints and teaching agents to check the second scan. In the first year of minor change, I’d set a calendar reminder to check our household reserve after each mortgage payment and keep it above four months of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job, careful with the household figures. A photograph of a door is not proof that it is the customer’s door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which photograph stuck with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the trainee the house number reflected in the van window. It was a different street, even though the front doors looked alike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rina (my wife) and I would top the reserve up after any repair before planning a holiday. That is a rule we can both see on the bank statement.

say: I’d say **door photographs** still need a street-number check.
I’d show agents the **second delivery scan** before closing a claim.
think: I think my **delivery work** continues in this mild world.
I count on my **usual wage** for the mortgage despite five months saved.
do: Keep **leading complaints** and teaching second-scan checks in 2026.
Replenish the **household reserve** after bills to keep four months of expenses saved.
feel: **Calm** about work, careful with household money.
S0.quote: A photograph of a door is not proof that it is the customer’s door.
fieldNote: The **five-month reserve** covers a repair but not lost wages indefinitely.
He treats **four months saved** as a household floor.

steps.text: Keep leading delivery complaints and teach agents to check second scans
Top up household reserve after bills whenever it falls below four months of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will take the easy delivery-status chats first. I would ask the manager for a written rota and the reopened-claim count before judging whether the new system saves work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the hard missing-parcel calls remain for a while, but my team could lose paid shifts as the first queue shrinks. Five months saved gives us time to look, not permission to take a lower weekly wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the original delivery scan beside each complaint and compare the new automated closure count with reopened claims during my paid shift. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid returns-supervisor role at a nearby centre only if written weekly wage and hours cover our mortgage, staying here until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours, though I can still check the figures. A shorter queue can mean a shorter pay packet for the same household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare twenty closed claims with the next week’s reopened list. I would take any repeated wrong-door cases to the manager with the original scan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the nearby role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the offer home and compare weekly pay, not just the job title. A longer drive also has to fit Rina’s school-kitchen hours and our children’s pickup.

say: I’d say **status chats** may move before hard missing-parcel calls.
I’d ask for **written rotas and reopenings** before calling automation a saving.
think: I think the **hard queue** may last longer.
I fear fewer **paid shifts** despite five months of savings.
do: Compare **twenty closed claims** with reopenings and original scans on paid time in 2026.
Apply for **posted returns-supervisor work** only with written mortgage-covering weekly wages/hours fitting Rina’s rota and pickup; stay until signed offer.
S1.quote: A shorter queue can mean a shorter pay packet for the same household.
fieldNote: He measures **reopened wrong-door cases** against automated closures.
The **five-month cushion** buys search time, not a wage cut.
A job move depends on **weekly pay**, travel and child pickup.

steps.text: Compare twenty automated closures with reopened claims and original delivery scans on paid shift
Apply for posted returns-supervisor work with written mortgage-covering weekly wages/hours; compare Rina’s rota and school pickup
Keep current job until a suitable offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 could decide a missing-parcel claim without opening the photograph. I would ask for written staffing dates and actual paid vacancies so people can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think cheap thinking AI could end my whole complaints queue in 2028. Robots around 2031 do not delay that screen-work risk, and five months saved would go quickly on mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d cancel the planned replacement of our working dining table and put that money in the reserve. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid warehouse-claims role only if its written weekly wage and hours cover our mortgage after travel and work with the school pickup; I’d keep my current job until a signed offer and take its required course only if funded on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but I still have a list of terms to check. Five months of savings is a cushion, not a second wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Rina (my wife) the table is scratched, not broken. If a leg becomes unsafe, we will repair it rather than buy a new set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need the actual vacancy, the first rota and paid training hours written down. If the course is just a suggestion, I will not spend our mortgage reserve on it.

say: I’d warn **2028 AGI** might decide missing-parcel claims without checking photographs.
I’d request **written dates and vacancies** for planning.
think: I think my **complaints queue** could end in 2028.
I know **five months saved** cannot replace a wage.
do: Cancel the **table replacement** while safe and save its price in 2026.
Apply for **posted warehouse claims** after 2028 only with written mortgage-covering pay/hours after travel and school-compatible shifts; stay until signed offer.
Take its **required course** only if funded on paid time for that posted paid vacancy.
S2.quote: Five months of savings is a cushion, not a second wage.
fieldNote: The **2028 thinking-AI deadline** reaches his screen work before robots.
The **safe table deferral** protects the reserve.
The job needs **net mortgage-covering pay**, workable pickup and funded paid-time training.

steps.text: Cancel dining-table replacement while old table is safe
Save dining-table money in the household reserve
Apply for posted warehouse-claims job; require written mortgage-covering net pay/hours, school pickup and signed offer
Take required funded warehouse-claims course on paid time only for posted paid vacancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives time to see whether a paid claims job is truly posted. I would tell agents to inspect the wage and rota before they enrol in anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn warehouse claims over five years if a real job needs it, though full AGI might also sort the paperwork. Rina and I can save more while I still have a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take an employer-funded warehouse-claims course on paid time only if a posted paid vacancy requires it, and add a fixed amount from each wage to our reserve. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for that role only if written weekly wage and hours cover our mortgage after travel and fit the children’s pickup, staying at the centre until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years lets me check a route instead of guessing. A training room cannot replace the family pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn in person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to trace a lost parcel through a warehouse handoff, not just learn the screen labels. If I cannot explain where responsibility changes, I am not ready to sign a claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which numbers matter at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the whole week of pay after fuel and the pickup time against Rina’s school rota. A few extra hourly coins can disappear on the drive.

say: I’d ask for a **posted claims wage** before training.
I’d ask for the **full rota** as well as the job title.
think: I think I could learn **warehouse claims** for a real role.
I know **full AGI** may also handle its paperwork.
do: Take **funded paid-time training** only if required for a posted paid warehouse-claims vacancy.
Save a **fixed amount** from each wage starting in 2026.
Apply for **posted claims work** after 2031 only with written mortgage-covering net pay/hours and school pickup; stay until signed offer.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to check a route.
S3.quote: A training room cannot replace the family pay packet.
fieldNote: He wants to trace a **warehouse handoff**, not memorize screens.
A **real posted vacancy** gates funded paid-time training.
He compares **pay after fuel** and school pickup times.

steps.text: Take employer-funded warehouse-claims course on paid time only if posted paid vacancy requires it
Save a fixed amount from each wage for mortgage reserve
Apply for posted claims job after 2031; require written mortgage-covering net pay/hours, pickup and signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us time to keep good delivery records and train new agents on real mistakes. I would keep a paid shadow call in the first week if the centre agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can earn and build a stronger reserve before 2036, but cheap thinking AI could still take the complaint decisions. Robots around 2039 are later and do not protect a headset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading delivery complaints and save a fixed amount after each pay. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for posted paid claims work only if my hours fall and its written weekly wage and hours cover the mortgage after travel and fit our child pickup, staying until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant change, steady enough about next year. Ten years before AGI lets me save without calling my job permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the shadow call work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would let a new agent hear a wrong-door call on a paid shift, then show the second scan. If the centre will not pay for that time, I cannot promise to do it after hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the children in their school unless Rina (my wife) and I had a signed offer with mortgage-covering pay after moving and travel costs. Some nearby jobs let us search before considering a move.

say: I’d ask the centre to pay for **shadow calls** when new agents join the team.
I’d keep **second-scan checks** in delivery complaints.
think: I think I can **earn and save** for years.
I know **2036 thinking AI** may still take complaint decisions.
do: Keep **complaints shifts**, save after payday and teach paid shadow calls only if the centre agrees.
Apply for **posted claims work** after 2036 if hours fall, with written mortgage-covering net pay/hours and school pickup; stay until signed offer.
Consider a **family move** only with a signed offer covering mortgage after moving/travel; search nearby before changing the children’s school.
S4.quote: Ten years before AGI lets me save without calling my job permanent.
fieldNote: A **paid shadow call** would teach a real wrong-door case.
A new role needs **net mortgage-covering pay** and workable pickup.

steps.text: Keep leading delivery complaints; give paid wrong-door shadow call to trainees only if centre agrees
Save a fixed amount after each pay for the mortgage reserve
Seek posted claims work if hours fall; require written mortgage-covering net pay/hours, pickup and signed offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could remove both the easy calls and my difficult queue in a short time. Five months saved helps us search but not replace a regular mortgage wage. I would need a posted paid role with written weekly wage and hours covering the mortgage, and a funded course on paid time if that role requires one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who verifies the door photograph after the software declares a parcel delivered. I need a person with paid time to look at the actual doorstep and correct the record.

headlineQuote: I need a person with paid time to look at the actual doorstep and correct the record.
portrait: At **43**, Emeka leads difficult delivery complaints after a two-year college diploma on typical pay.
He and Rina support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with five months saved.
He avoids **AI tools** and checks the original delivery record.
He weighs **real posted jobs** against weekly pay, hours and family travel.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his complaints wage and exhaust five months of savings before a replacement job begins.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted paid role** with written mortgage-covering pay and hours and required funded paid-time training would help.
